passage:
"I never said I'd pick you up," Farhan said. "You always twist things."
"You texted, 'I'll be there by six.' I have it right here."
"That was about the library. You're making it about you again. This is exactly why I get upset, Ganga."
Ganga opened her mouth, then closed it. "Sorry," she said, and hated that she had.
That night, at her sister's flat, she said, "Didi, this is the fourth time. I say what happened, he says it didn't, and I end up apologising."
"Do you write things down?"
"I've started. Dates, and what each of us said."
"Then keep going. That's not you being oversensitive. Come here more often and tell me what's happening."
Ganga nodded slowly. "It's not my fault. Is it?"
"It's not."

qa.a: He had texted, "I'll be there by six."

qa.q: Why did Ganga say sorry even though she had the message?
qa.a: She felt confused and guilty, because Farhan turned the argument round until she seemed to be at fault. She hated apologising even as she did it.
She can keep her dated notes, keep talking to her sister and other trusted people outside the relationship, and trust her own memory of what happened.

qa.q: How does Ganga's sister see the situation?
qa.a: Didi sees a pattern in which Ganga's account is denied and she ends up apologising. She tells Ganga this is not oversensitivity and not her fault.

grounding: A partner twists the protagonist's words so she feels confused and guilty; she starts keeping notes and talks to her sister.

passage:
March 3: Jagdish told Thomas he felt left out when Thomas skipped his graduation dinner. By the end of the talk Thomas was saying, 'So now I'm a terrible partner?' and Jagdish was the one apologising, unsure how the conversation had turned.
March 17: It happened again over a missed call. That night Jagdish opened a notes page on his phone and wrote down what he had said, word for word, and what came back.
April 2: Reading two weeks of notes, Jagdish saw the same shape each time: his worry became his fault. He showed them to his older sister, Shalini, over tea. She read quietly and said, 'You're not imagining this, and none of it is on you.' Jagdish felt steadier than he had in months, and booked a session with the college counsellor for Friday.

qa.q: What did Jagdish start writing down on March 17?
qa.a: Jagdish wrote down what he had said, word for word, and what came back.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling at the end of the March 3 talk?
qa.a: Jagdish felt confused and guilty, apologising even though he was the one who had raised a hurt.

qa.q: What small step helped Jagdish trust his own memory?
qa.a: Keeping word-for-word notes and showing them to Shalini, someone outside the relationship, made the pattern visible.

qa.q: How might Thomas see these arguments?
qa.a: Thomas seems to hear Jagdish's hurt as an attack and turns it back, so in Thomas's version the problem becomes Jagdish's complaint rather than the skipped dinner.

grounding: Shows a partner twisting words until Jagdish feels at fault, and the steps of noticing the pattern, keeping notes, confiding in family and trusting his own perception.

passage: Jatin, sit. Your Sumit Mama is going to tell you something I never told your mother properly. At twenty-one I was seeing a girl from my typing class, Rekha. If I said I was tired, she said I was bored of her. If I said I wasn't bored, she said I was calling her a liar. I went home feeling guilty for things I hadn't done. One evening my friend Iqbal asked, 'Why do you always say sorry after meeting her?' That question stuck in me. I began writing in a small notebook what I had actually said each day. After a month I read it back and saw the same trick on every page. I trusted that notebook more than the fog in my head, and I ended it. So when your friends say something feels off, listen to them, Jatin.

qa.a: Sumit met Rekha in the typing class.

qa.q: How did young Sumit feel after meeting Rekha?
qa.a: Sumit felt guilty and confused, going home sorry for things he had not done.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Sumit see the pattern?
qa.a: Writing down what he had actually said each day and reading a month of it back, which let him trust the record over his confusion.

qa.q: What was it like for Iqbal watching Sumit back then?
qa.a: Iqbal noticed Sumit apologising after every meeting and was concerned enough to ask why, which gave Sumit the first push.

grounding: An uncle recalls a partner who turned his words around, and how noticing the pattern, keeping notes and listening to a friend helped him trust his own perception.
